subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 56-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. Blood pressure is 78/50 mm Hg, pulse is 122/min, and his neck veins are distended. Auscultation of the heart reveals faint, distant heart sounds. Chest x-ray shows a normal mediastinal width and clear lung fields with symmetric breath sounds.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tension pneumothorax
Cardiac tamponade
Constrictive pericarditis
Cardiogenic shock from acute myocardial infarction
Distributive shock from sepsis

explanation_correct: The triad of hypotension, distended neck veins, and distant (muffled) heart sounds is the Beck triad of cardiac tamponade, in which compression of the heart by fluid (eg, blood after trauma) decreases cardiac output and diastolic pressures equilibrate in all four chambers. Other findings include increased heart rate, pulsus paradoxus, low-voltage QRS ± electrical alternans on ECG, and effusion with systolic RA and diastolic RV collapse on echocardiography.

explanation_incorrect.A: Tension pneumothorax causes distended neck veins and hypotension, but it produces hyperresonance with absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation on the affected side; this patient has clear lungs with symmetric breath sounds.
explanation_incorrect.C: Constrictive pericarditis is a chronic condition with a prominent y descent on the jugular venous pulse and a pericardial knock, not an acute post-traumatic triad of distant heart sounds.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cardiogenic shock from MI would show ischemic ECG changes and elevated left-sided filling pressures; it does not cause distant heart sounds or jugular distention from pericardial fluid compression.
explanation_incorrect.E: Distributive shock from sepsis presents with warm, dry skin and systemic vasodilation, not the mechanical compression findings and distant heart sounds of tamponade.

educationalObjective: Beck triad — hypotension, distended neck veins, and distant heart sounds — is the classic presentation of cardiac tamponade.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 62-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer presents with progressive dyspnea and light-headedness. Blood pressure is 86/54 mm Hg with a fall in systolic pressure of 14 mm Hg during inspiration, and pulse is 118/min. Electrocardiogram shows low-voltage QRS complexes whose amplitudes vary from beat to beat in a regular alternating pattern. Neck veins are distended and heart sounds are distant.
question: Which of the following best explains the electrocardiographic finding?

options.text: "Swinging" movement of the heart within a large pericardial effusion (electrical alternans)
Alternating conduction over fast and slow atrioventricular nodal pathways
Retrograde conduction through an accessory pathway
Diffuse myocardial infiltration with amyloid protein
Hypokalemia-induced repolarization changes

explanation_correct: In cardiac tamponade, ECG may show low-voltage QRS complexes and/or electrical alternans, which is due to the "swinging" movement of the heart within a large pericardial effusion. Combined with the Beck triad components and pulsus paradoxus (an inspiratory systolic pressure fall > 10 mm Hg), the diagnosis is secure, and treatment is pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage.

explanation_incorrect.B: Dual AV nodal pathway physiology underlies AV nodal reentrant tachycardia and does not produce beat-to-beat alternation of QRS amplitude during sinus rhythm.
explanation_incorrect.C: An accessory pathway causes preexcitation (short PR, delta wave) or reentrant tachycardias such as AVRT, not regular beat-to-beat variation in QRS voltage.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amyloid infiltration causes a low-voltage ECG in restrictive cardiomyopathy, but it does not produce the characteristic regular amplitude alternation from a swinging heart within an effusion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hypokalemia produces ST depression, flattened T waves, and prominent U waves; it does not cause alternating QRS amplitudes.

educationalObjective: In cardiac tamponade, low-voltage QRS with electrical alternans results from the swinging motion of the heart within a large pericardial effusion.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 47-year-old man with uremic pericarditis develops progressive dyspnea, hypotension, and distended neck veins. Heart sounds are distant, and systolic blood pressure falls by 12 mm Hg during inspiration. Echocardiography is ordered to confirm the suspected diagnosis.
question: Which of the following findings is most consistent with cardiac tamponade on this evaluation?

options.text: Prominent y descent on the jugular venous pulse
Diastolic collapse of the right ventricle
Hyperresonance with absent breath sounds on the left
Kussmaul sign on neck vein inspection
Pathologic Q waves in the inferior leads

explanation_correct: Echocardiography in cardiac tamponade shows pericardial effusion, systolic RA collapse, and diastolic RV collapse, reflecting the elevated intrapericardial pressure overcoming chamber filling pressures — combined with IVC plethora. Diastolic RV collapse is a hallmark confirmatory finding in this uremic pericarditis patient with pulsus paradoxus and Beck triad elements.

explanation_incorrect.A: A prominent y descent is seen in constrictive pericarditis; in tamponade the y descent is absent because atrial emptying into the compressed ventricle is impaired.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hyperresonance with absent breath sounds indicates tension pneumothorax, a different cause of obstructive shock that compresses the heart from outside the pleural space.
explanation_incorrect.D: Kussmaul sign (a paradoxical rise in JVP with inspiration) is classically associated with constrictive pericarditis, not tamponade.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pathologic Q waves signify prior transmural myocardial infarction and are unrelated to pericardial fluid compression physiology.

educationalObjective: Echocardiography in tamponade shows pericardial effusion, systolic RA collapse, diastolic RV collapse, and IVC plethora; the JVP y descent is absent.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 39-year-old man with a large pericardial effusion from tuberculous pericarditis is monitored at the bedside. During quiet inspiration, his systolic blood pressure falls from 110 mm Hg to 94 mm Hg, and the fall reverses promptly during expiration.
question: Which of the following sequences best explains the exaggerated inspiratory fall in his systolic blood pressure?

options.text: Inspiration decreases venous return to the right ventricle, reducing pulmonary output and left ventricular filling
Inspiration mechanically compresses the aorta against the vertebral column, directly lowering measured pressure
Inspiration increases right ventricular filling; the interventricular septum bows toward the left ventricle (due to decreased pericardial compliance), reducing left ventricular ejection volume
Inspiration augments sympathetic outflow, increasing contractility and provoking pulsus alternans
The freely expanding pericardium permits exaggerated filling of all four chambers, diluting the stroke volume

explanation_correct: Pulsus paradoxus is a decrease in the amplitude of systolic blood pressure by more than 10 mm Hg during inspiration (a 16 mm Hg fall here). Increased venous return during inspiration increases RV filling; in a tamponaded heart with decreased pericardial compliance, the interventricular septum bows toward the LV, reducing LV ejection volume and therefore systolic blood pressure.

explanation_incorrect.A: Venous return to the right ventricle increases (not decreases) during inspiration; the reduced LV ejection is secondary to septal shift, not to diminished pulmonary output.
explanation_incorrect.B: Direct mechanical compression of the aorta by inspiration is not the mechanism; the fall in systolic pressure reflects decreased LV ejection volume.
explanation_incorrect.D: The inspiratory pressure drop is a mechanical filling phenomenon, not a sympathetic inotropic effect, and pulsus alternans is a separate finding of severe left ventricular failure.
explanation_incorrect.E: In tamponade the pericardium is constrained (decreased compliance), not freely expanding; the four chambers share a fixed volume, which is precisely why RV filling displaces the septum toward the LV.

educationalObjective: Pulsus paradoxus: inspiration increases RV filling, the septum bows toward the LV (decreased pericardial compliance), LV ejection volume falls, and systolic BP drops more than 10 mm Hg.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 9-year-old boy hospitalized for a severe asthma exacerbation is found to have a fall in systolic blood pressure from 112 mm Hg to 98 mm Hg during inspiration. His physician explains that, beyond pericardial disease, this finding is classically associated with certain pulmonary conditions.
question: Which of the following sets of conditions is classically associated with this finding?

options.text: Aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, atrial myxoma
Croup, obstructive sleep apnea, asthma, COPD
Ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus
Coarctation of the aorta, aortic regurgitation, thyrotoxicosis
Endocardial fibroelastosis, Löffler endocarditis, amyloidosis

explanation_correct: Pulsus paradoxus — a decrease in systolic blood pressure amplitude of more than 10 mm Hg during inspiration — is seen in constrictive pericarditis, obstructive pulmonary disease, and cardiac tamponade. The obstructive pulmonary diseases group together by the mnemonic pea COAT: Croup, OSA, Asthma, COPD (with Tamponade), which is why this asthmatic child exhibits the finding.

explanation_incorrect.A: Aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, and atrial myxoma produce murmurs and embolic phenomena but are not classic causes of an exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic pressure.
explanation_incorrect.C: VSD, ASD, and PDA are left-to-right shunt lesions; they cause volume overload and murmurs, not pulsus paradoxus.
explanation_incorrect.D: Aortic regurgitation produces a wide pulse pressure with a water-hammer (bounding) pulse — the opposite of an inspiratory collapse in systolic pressure — and thyrotoxicosis is a cause of high-output heart failure, not pulsus paradoxus.
explanation_incorrect.E: Endocardial fibroelastosis, Löffler endocarditis, and amyloidosis are restrictive/infiltrative cardiomyopathies causing diastolic dysfunction, not the classic pulsus paradoxus triad of conditions.

educationalObjective: Pulsus paradoxus is seen in constrictive pericarditis, obstructive pulmonary disease (Croup, OSA, Asthma, COPD — pea COAT), and cardiac tamponade.
